name: Robert Capa Contemporary Photography Center
description: A photography centre at Nagymező utca 8, established in 2013, the centenary year of Robert Capa's birth and set in an Art Nouveau house of 1912. It holds a large collection of Capa prints, shows permanent displays on Capa and André Kertész, and runs temporary exhibitions, workshops and the annual Capa Grand Prize.

children.text: The Robert Capa Contemporary Photography Center at Nagymező utca 8 in Terézváros was established by the Hungarian State on 12 July 2013 and opened on 3 December 2013, in the centenary year of Robert Capa's birth. Capa was a Hungarian-American photographer, and the state acquired his legacy in 2008 and brought it back to Hungary. That led to the plan for a photography institution. A selection of about 30 images was first shown at the Hungarian National Museum in March 2009, and the collection was later shown at the Ludwig Museum.

The centre holds more than 900 prints of Capa's photographs, together with 48 vintage prints that cover his career. Cornell Capa and the writer Richard Whelan selected the prints from the negatives and three sets were made; the other two are at the International Center of Photography in New York and the Fuji Art Museum in Tokyo. The centre's site lists two permanent exhibitions, Robert Capa – The Photojournalist and André Kertész – The Sentimentalist. It also organises temporary exhibitions, workshops and the annual Robert Capa Photography Grand Prize.

The house itself is part of the interest. It is an Art Nouveau building from 1912 commissioned by the art collector Lajos Ernst; Wikipedia credits it to the architect Gyula Fodor. The staircase has a large glass window by Miksa Róth, based on designs by the painter József Rippl-Rónai, and the stone benches were designed by Ödön Lechner. The Ernst Museum, which showed Ernst's private collection, occupied the building until August 2013. After Ernst's death in 1937 the cultural institution here changed names several times, and for decades the house served as a branch of the Kunsthalle.

Nagymező utca is also home to the Mai Manó House at number 20, so the centre pairs naturally with that house of photography on the same street. The Capa Center's site lists an event hall, the 8F Gallery and the Robert Capa Café on the premises.
Good to know
The centre is at Nagymező utca 8 in District VI, on the same street as the Mai Manó House at number 20.
Exhibitions change, so check the official site for current opening times, tickets and which temporary shows are on.
The centre's site lists a separate exhibition in the 8F Gallery; check the official site for what is on view on which days.
The permanent exhibition on Capa shows 140 prints according to Wikipedia; check the official site for the current display.

historyIntro: The Robert Capa Centre celebrates the contribution of Hungarian photographers to international visual storytelling, especially documentary images.

historySections.heading: A centre named for a Budapest-born photographer

children.text: Robert Capa, born in Budapest in 1913, became one of the most influential war photographers of the twentieth century. The photography centre opened during the centenary year of his birth to recognise photographers and the power of their work.

The centre presents contemporary exhibitions, often including press and documentary photography. In these images, history is not only a collection of dates but the records of how individuals witnessed moments of conflict, change and ordinary life.

name: Mai Manó House
description: Built in 1894 at Nagymező utca 20 as the multi-storey studio of the court photographer Manó Mai, this neo-Renaissance house keeps its decorated facade, glass-roofed studio and Zsolnay details. Since 1999 the House of Hungarian Photography has used it for exhibitions and a photography library.

children.text: Mai Manó House at Nagymező utca 20 was built as a purpose-designed photographic studio. Manó Mai (1855–1917), known for his child portraits, received the title of imperial and royal court photographer in 1885 and became an independent photographer in Budapest in 1878. He photographed the funeral procession of Lajos Kossuth in 1894 and Béla Bartók in 1903, and won a gold medal at the 1900 Paris World Exhibition. In 1906 he launched the periodical A Fény (The Light), which was edited from the same house.

Mai and his wife bought a one-storey house on the site in January 1892, and in January 1893 he applied for a permit to demolish it and build a new studio house. The plans were drawn by Rezső Nay and Muki Strausz, József Mann was the master builder, and the residence permit was granted on 31 July 1894. The building has eight levels that appear as three storeys from outside. The neo-Renaissance facade has statues, reliefs, ornaments and frescoes on terracotta tiles, with allegorical figures representing painting and photography. Inside are a carved oak staircase, stained glass by Miksa Róth and a Sunlight Studio with a glass balcony and slanted glass roof, whose street-side niches use Zsolnay pyrogranite.

After Mai's death, Hugó Weisz of Arad took over running the house. In 1931 Sándor Rozsnyai and his wife Mici, known as Miss Arizona, bought it from the photographer's son and built the Arizona Club in the courtyard, which operated until 1944. The Manó Mai Gallery opened on the mezzanine in 1995, and the Foundation of Hungarian Photography began buying lease rights from tenants in 1996. On 18 March 1999 the House of Hungarian Photography opened on the first and second floors.

Today the building holds exhibition halls, the József Pécsi Photography Library and offices, and the Library network page notes that parts of it still need restoration. Its official site lists current, future and past exhibitions, a bookshop and a library, and it is operated as part of the Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest.
Good to know
The house is at Nagymező utca 20 in District VI, on the same street as the Robert Capa Contemporary Photography Center at number 8.
Look at the facade before you go in: the statues, reliefs and allegorical figures of painting and photography are part of the 1894 design.
Check the official Mai Manó House site for current exhibitions, opening times and tickets, because the programme changes.
Parts of the building are still awaiting restoration, so not every historic room is necessarily accessible; ask or check before visiting.

historyIntro: Mai Manó House is itself a historic photographic artefact: an elaborate nineteenth-century studio created for a professional portrait photographer.

children.text: Hungarian photographer Mai Manó commissioned the building in 1894 on Nagymező Street. Its richly decorated staircases, stained glass and monogrammed ironwork reflect the social standing of studio portrait photography in that era.
The house is now used for photography exhibitions, books and research. Its survival allows visitors to see how the profession once presented itself architecturally as well as through photographs.

stories.title: The studio owner's initials in the stairs

children.text: The visitor account points out the 'MM' monogram on the ornamental staircase railings. It is a small detail that connects today's exhibition visitor with the photographer who had the building made.

name: Vasarely Museum Budapest
description: Set in an outbuilding of Óbuda's baroque Zichy Mansion, this museum is devoted to Victor Vasarely, the Hungarian-born artist often called the grandfather of Op art. Its rooms follow him from early advertising graphics to the geometric and kinetic works of the 1960s and 1970s, with temporary shows alongside.

children.text: The Vasarely Museum stands on Szentlélek tér in Óbuda, in a wing of the Zichy Mansion complex beside the Danube. The mansion itself is an 18th-century baroque building, and the museum occupies the former storage building of the palace rather than the main house, which today holds the Kassák Museum. Next door in the other outbuildings is the Óbuda Museum, so one walk can cover three quite different collections.

Victor Vasarely was born Győző Vásárhelyi in Pécs in 1906 and left Hungary for Paris in 1930. Before that he studied in Sándor Bortnyik's workshop in Budapest, a school shaped by Bauhaus ideas of visual education. In France he met the gallerist Denise René in 1944 and, from 1947, focused on the geometric and optical abstraction that made him famous. His 1937 painting Zebra is regarded by some as one of the earliest examples of Op art.

The Budapest museum grew out of gifts that Vasarely made to Hungarian institutions. One guide notes that Vasarely gave works to the Museum of Fine Arts several times after 1959. The museum opened in 1987. The collection is usually described as numbering more than 400 works, a figure that includes both original pieces and reproduced editions.

Inside, the display traces his path from academic drawings and advertising graphics of his early years to the Op art and kinetic pieces of the 1960s and 1970s. Look for the way flat patterns appear to swell, tilt or vibrate as you move past them; that effect is the point of the work, and it is why the museum rewards slow walking. The building also hosts temporary exhibitions, including solo and group shows with Hungarian and international artists.

Vasarely is honoured elsewhere too. A museum in his birthplace Pécs was established in 1976, and the Fondation Vasarely in Aix-en-Provence also opened in 1976 in a building he designed. Seeing the Óbuda collection gives a Hungarian view of an artist who spent most of his life in France.
Good to know
Check the official Vasarely Museum site for current opening times, tickets and temporary exhibitions before you go.
The Kassák Museum and the Óbuda Museum share the Zichy Mansion complex, so they combine easily into one visit.
The museum is on Szentlélek tér in Óbuda; use the BudapestGo journey planner to find the best public transport route from your hotel.

historyIntro: The Vasarely Museum offers a journey into Op Art, where colour and geometry make a flat image appear to vibrate or move.

historySections.heading: A Hungarian-born pioneer of optical art

children.text: Victor Vasarely helped shape the twentieth-century movement known as Op Art. His experiments with patterned shapes and colour relationships challenged the viewer's perception without relying on conventional illusionistic painting.

The Budapest museum introduces his work in Óbuda and explains his ambition to make modern visual art approachable. The collection forms part of a wider story connecting Hungarian artists with the international avant-garde.

name: Madame Tussauds Budapest
description: Madame Tussauds Budapest fills the Palazzo Dorottya in downtown Pest, between Vörösmarty Square and the Danube promenade. It presents wax figures of Hungarian and international personalities in themed settings, including a recreated Buda Castle tunnel, and Hungarian craftspeople built many of the surrounding sets.

children.text: Madame Tussauds Budapest is in downtown Pest, not in the Castle District. It occupies the Palazzo Dorottya at Dorottya utca 6, in a building that stands between Vörösmarty Square and the Danube riverside promenade. The attraction opened on 25 May 2023 and covers about 2,000 square metres according to a report in the Budapest Times.

The route is built around themed zones with around fifty figures. Hungarian history and culture are represented by figures such as Lajos Kossuth, Empress Sissi, King Stephen I, Sándor Petőfi, Mihály Munkácsy and Ferenc Liszt. Sport and entertainment bring in Ferenc Puskás, László Papp, Béla Lugosi, Katinka Hosszú and Harry Houdini, while international singers, film actors, politicians and royal figures fill other rooms. The figures were chosen after market research and negotiations over the rights to use them.

Several settings are Budapest scenes recreated indoors. Press coverage of the opening names a Buda Castle Tunnel, a meeting with stars on the Danube embankment, a helicopter filming scene on Fisherman's Bastion and a themed world of spas. Interactive screens, light and sound effects and selfie points are part of the design.

According to We Love Budapest, each figure was made by about twenty artists at a workshop near London, taking three to four months, and the hair alone took six weeks. The sets around them were made in Hungary by stained-glass artists, architectural sculptors, woodcarvers, ornamental tinsmiths, gilders and theatre and film set designers.

The brand goes back to Anna Marie Tussaud (1761-1850), a French artist who specialised in life-size figures of famous people. Her first permanent exhibition opened on Baker Street in London in 1835. The Budapest venue is a recent addition to that tradition, and its 17 Hungarian figures, out of 51 in total according to We Love Budapest, give it a local character.
Good to know
Check the official Madame Tussauds Budapest site for current opening times and tickets; popular periods can fill up.
The entrance is on Dorottya utca, a short walk from Vörösmarty Square, so it fits easily into a downtown Pest walk.
Figure line-ups change over time; confirm on the official site which personalities are on display before you go.

historyIntro: Madame Tussauds Budapest is a recent attraction in an older building: a wax-figure exhibition that opened in 2023 inside the Palazzo Dorottya, a Pest house that stood empty for almost a decade before its renovation.

historySections.heading: From London waxworks to a global brand

children.text: The name comes from Anna Marie Tussaud (1761-1850), a French artist who specialised in life-size figures of famous people. According to Wikipedia, she opened her first permanent exhibition on Baker Street in London in 1835, after decades of touring. That idea, a gallery of recognisable personalities modelled in wax, is the one the Budapest attraction continues, with figures chosen after market research and negotiations over the right to portray each person.

The exhibition is in the Palazzo Dorottya at Dorottya utca 6, in Pest beside Vörösmarty Square. Hungarian architectural press knows the building as the former Wurm House and refers to it as the Pollack-Hauszmann building. Before its renovation it was unoccupied for almost a decade. The project was commissioned by RDM, a group of Italian investors, and led by the Zoboki Demeter and Partners architectural office, with a facade refresh and restoration of the building's original look. Afterwards the lower storeys held a garage and commercial spaces and the upper floors offices and residential units.

Madame Tussauds Budapest opened on 25 May 2023, filling about 2,000 square metres of the palazzo. Reports on the opening describe a red carpet route past around fifty figures. We Love Budapest reported that each figure was made by about twenty artists at a workshop near London, taking three to four months, and that Hungarian craftspeople, including stained-glass artists, architectural sculptors, woodcarvers and set designers, made the settings. Press coverage also noted that organisers asked the public which personalities they most wanted to see.
